summary.text: 风 means “wind” or “moving air” and is the simplified form of 風. A bird-shaped sign was used for the word “wind”; one proposal is that it was reused because the bird’s name and “wind” sounded alike, but the bird’s referent and spoken name are uncertain. In later 風, 凡 is analyzed as a sound component, while the lower marks are interpreted as traces of tail feathers.

formation.text: The later form 風 is analyzed as phonosemantic: 凡 supplies a proposed phonetic cue, and the lower marks are interpreted as pictorial traces of feathers from the earlier bird-shaped graph. The earlier whole bird sign was used for “wind”; sound-based reuse is proposed because the bird-name and “wind” may have sounded alike, but the bird’s name and that match are unverified.

components.text: 凡 is analyzed as the phonetic component in 風. Old Chinese reconstructions give related but nonidentical readings, suggesting a sound relationship; this comparison alone does not establish the graphic analysis.

sound_limitation.text: These reconstructions provide sound comparisons but do not by themselves establish 凡’s graphic identity or role in 風.

sound.text: The Baxter–Sagart reconstructions are related but nonidentical.

components.text: In 風, the lower marks shaped as 虫 are interpreted as bird-tail feather traces, not as an original insect element. Chu forms preserve differing feather designs; Qin forms reshape them as 虫, a shape continued in seal script. The Han-period insect explanation records a later interpretation.

history.text: Late Shang divinations are reported to use a bird-shaped graph for the word “wind.” A proposed transition drops other bird details while retaining 凡 and feather marks, but this intermediate stage is inferred across an interval without cited examples. Chu forms preserve varying feather marks; Qin forms reshape them as 虫, a shape continued in seal script. The Han-period Shuowen account explains 風 through insects and analyzes it as 虫 plus phonetic 凡; this records a later understanding of the graph, not its original construction.
风 is the simplified form of 風. The proposed change of its lower part from 䖝 to 㐅 is not established by the account of the traditional graph’s development.

uncertainties.text: The early bird graph’s referent and spoken name are uncertain. Green peafowl has been proposed, but clear oracle-bone uses of the graph for that animal are disputed or lacking. The proposed sound-based borrowing therefore does not demonstrate that the bird’s name resembled the word for wind.

The transition from the early bird graph to the later 凡-and-feather form is inferred across an interval without cited intermediate examples. The specific graphic pathway to simplified 风 is also unresolved.

senses.text: Older dictionary material records these senses, but does not establish their dates or a development from “wind.”
In modern Chinese, 风 means wind or air.

limitations.text: The evidence does not establish when customs, demeanor, style, atmosphere, trends, or news became senses of 風, or how these uses relate to one another or to “wind.”

overview.text: 风 means “wind” and is the simplified form of 風. A bird-shaped sign may have been reused for “wind” because the old bird-name and “wind” may have sounded alike; the bird’s spoken name is unknown, so that match is unverified. In 風, 凡 combines with marks interpreted as feathers.

components.text: The nonidentical Old Chinese forms suggest a historical sound relationship for 凡 and 風, but the comparison alone does not establish 凡’s role in 風.
In 風, the marks shaped as 虫 are interpreted as reshaped feather traces, rather than as an original insect element.
